title: 2027 Medicare Deductible Rises to $1,776: Build the Patient-Responsibility Budget by Entity From the Books, Split Implicit Price Concessions From Medicare Bad Debt, and Start the 120-Day Clock on Every January Bill

mainEntity.name: What is the 2027 Medicare Part A deductible and when does it apply?

acceptedAnswer.text: The 2027 inpatient hospital deductible is $1,776, up $40 from $1,736 in 2026, with daily coinsurance of $444 for days 61 through 90, $888 for lifetime reserve days, and $222 for skilled nursing facility days 21 through 100. CMS announced the amounts on November 17, 2026 and published them in the Federal Register on November 19. They take effect January 1, 2027 and apply to benefit periods that begin in 2027.

mainEntity.name: Does the Medicare Part A deductible reset on January 1 like the Part B deductible?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. The Part A deductible is charged once per benefit period, which begins on admission and ends after 60 consecutive days without inpatient or skilled nursing care, so a patient can owe it more than once in a year or not at all. The Part B deductible, $292 in 2027, is annual and resets on January 1, which is why physician practices and outpatient departments see patient responsibility spike in the first quarter.

mainEntity.name: Can a physician practice claim Medicare bad debt on an unpaid Part B deductible?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Medicare bad debt reimbursement under 42 CFR 413.89 is claimed on the cost report, and a practice paid under the physician fee schedule does not file one. Hospitals, critical access hospitals, skilled nursing facilities, and hospital-based outpatient departments can claim unpaid Medicare deductibles and coinsurance at 65 percent of the allowable amount after a documented collection effort. A practice's unpaid Part B deductible is an implicit price concession it absorbs in full.

mainEntity.name: Is an unpaid Medicare deductible bad debt expense or a reduction of revenue?

acceptedAnswer.text: For most providers it is a reduction of revenue. Under ASC 606, when a provider bills a patient without assessing credit at the start of the encounter, the share it does not expect to collect is an implicit price concession that reduces the transaction price and net patient service revenue at the date of service. Bad debt expense under ASC 326 applies only where the provider expected full payment at inception and the account was later impaired. CMS separately requires Medicare bad debt write-offs to go to an uncollectible receivable account that reduces revenue, not to a contractual allowance.

mainEntity.name: How much of an unpaid Medicare deductible does Medicare pay back through the cost report?

acceptedAnswer.text: 65 percent of the allowable amount, less sequestration. To be allowable the debt must relate to covered services, consist of a deductible or coinsurance, and be written off after a reasonable collection effort of at least 120 days from the first bill, with the clock restarting after each payment. For dual eligible patients the provider must bill the state Medicaid agency and may claim the unpaid balance after the state remittance without further collection effort. The claim goes on the cost report for the period in which the account is written off.

content:
CMS set the 2027 Medicare deductible at $1,776 per inpatient benefit period and $292 for Part B, effective January 1. The $40 and $9 increases are small. The money is in who owes each deductible, what share you expect to collect, and whether every unpaid dollar is a price concession or a Medicare bad debt.

Why this matters now

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services published its 2027 Medicare Parts A and B premiums and deductibles fact sheet on 2026-11-17. The inpatient hospital deductible rises from $1,736 to $1,776, daily coinsurance for days 61 through 90 rises from $434 to $444, lifetime reserve days from $868 to $888, and skilled nursing facility coinsurance for days 21 through 100 from $217 to $222. The Part B annual deductible rises from $283 to $292 and the standard Part B premium from $202.90 to $209.40. CMS attributes the Part B change mainly to projected increases in healthcare spending. The two Federal Register notices that make the amounts binding, CMS-8092-N for Part A and CMS-8094-N for Part B, were published on 2026-11-19 and take effect January 1, 2027. The Part A notice projects 5.68 million inpatient deductibles, 1.32 million coinsurance days, 0.66 million lifetime reserve days, and 27.50 million SNF coinsurance days in 2027, and puts the aggregate cost to beneficiaries at about $770 million.

The timing matters more than the amounts. On 2026-11-04 Kodiak Solutions reported that the 2,400 hospitals on its platform wrote off $52.1 billion to bad debt and final denials in 2025, up 17.6 percent and about 10 percent of net revenue, and extrapolated the national figure to $132.2 billion. HFMA's analysis of 2026-11-17 puts bad debt at roughly two thirds of that leakage and notes that the share has barely moved since 2023 despite the technology spent on it. Beneficiary coverage of the new amounts, including Fortune on 2026-11-27, explains what a patient will owe and when the Part A trust fund runs short. None of it tells a hospital group or a practice with three entities what the reset does to its patient receivable in January, which unpaid dollars Medicare will give back through the cost report, and how the budget should carry each line. That is this article.

What changes on January 1 and who actually owes it

A Medicare deductible is not revenue the provider gains or loses. For an inpatient stay under Original Medicare, the hospital's expected payment for the case is set by the DRG. Medicare pays that amount less the deductible and coinsurance, and the beneficiary owes the rest. The deductible therefore moves dollars between two payers with very different collection rates: Medicare, which pays nearly all of what it owes within weeks, and the patient, a secondary insurer, or a state Medicaid agency, which pay some of it, slowly. Every change in the deductible is a change in payer mix inside the same case.

Two features of the schedule decide where the January effect lands. The Part A deductible is charged per benefit period, which begins on admission and ends after 60 consecutive days without inpatient or skilled nursing care, so the $1,776 amount applies to benefit periods that begin in 2027 and there is no calendar reset. The Part B deductible is annual and does reset on January 1. For a physician practice or a hospital outpatient department, every Original Medicare patient walks in on January 2 owing up to $292 before the 20 percent coinsurance starts, and the first Part B provider that patient sees is the one that bills it. That is why a practice's patient-responsibility share of Part B revenue jumps in the first quarter and falls back by April, and why January patient receivables age worse than any other month.

Who owes the deductible is a question the books can answer. Medicare Advantage members are outside this schedule entirely, because plans set their own cost sharing, so the exposure scales with the Original Medicare share of each entity's payer mix. Beneficiaries with a Medigap policy have the Part A deductible paid by the secondary insurer under most plans, while Plan G, the broadest plan still open to new enrollees, pays the Part A deductible but leaves the Part B deductible with the patient. Dual eligible beneficiaries have their cost sharing billed to the state Medicaid agency, which in most states pays little or none of it. Patients with Original Medicare and no secondary coverage owe the full amount. Each of those groups has a different expected collection rate, and the budget should carry them as separate lines, not one.

One hospital group worked through, entity by entity

Call the group Riverbend Health: a 220-bed hospital, an employed physician group, and a skilled nursing facility, each in its own QuickBooks company file, consolidated monthly. The figures are illustrative. The question for each entity is the same: how many 2027 deductibles and coinsurance days will it bill, to whom, what share will it collect, and how much of the shortfall Medicare will reimburse through the cost report.

Riverbend Medical Center: 3,600 inpatient deductibles

The 2026 claims data shows 4,000 Original Medicare inpatient discharges, of which 3,600 started a new benefit period and carried a deductible. The remittance and secondary-payer fields in the patient accounting system split those 3,600 into 1,980 with a Medigap or other secondary payer, 720 dual eligibles, and 900 with no secondary coverage. At $1,776 each, the 2027 deductible base is $6.39 million: $3.52 million owed by secondary insurers, $1.28 million billed to the state, and $1.60 million billed to patients.

The secondary-insurer line collects at close to 100 percent and the budget treats it as insured revenue. The state line collects at nearly zero, because the state's liability under its lesser-of rule is usually nothing once the Medicare payment exceeds the Medicaid rate. After the state remittance comes back, the unpaid $1.28 million is a Medicare crossover bad debt, allowable without further collection effort, and the cost report returns 65 percent, or $831,000, leaving $448,000 with the hospital. The patient line is where judgment lives. Riverbend's three-year history shows it collects 45 percent of self-pay-after-Medicare deductibles. Because it bills those patients without a credit assessment, the 55 percent it does not expect to collect, $879,000, is an implicit price concession under ASC 606: a reduction of revenue at the date of service, not an expense. Of that $879,000, the portion that completes a documented 120-day collection effort and is written off becomes allowable Medicare bad debt. Riverbend documents the effort on 90 percent of accounts, so $791,000 is allowable and the cost report returns 65 percent, $514,000. The hospital keeps a net shortfall of $365,000 on the patient line.

Now the increase. The $40 rise moves $144,000 from Medicare to the three other payers. On the secondary line it costs nothing. On the state line it costs 35 percent of $28,800, about $10,000. On the patient line it costs 55 percent uncollected less 65 percent recovered on the 90 percent that is documented, about $8,000. The headline change costs Riverbend Medical Center roughly $18,000 in 2027. Compare that with the 120-day log. If documentation slips from 90 percent of accounts to 60 percent, allowable bad debt falls to $527,000 and the recovery to $343,000, a loss of $171,000. The collection log is worth nine times the rate change.

Riverbend Physicians: the January reset with no cost report behind it

The physician group sees about 12,000 Original Medicare patients in a first quarter. Its claims history shows it is the first Part B provider of the year for 35 percent of them, so 4,200 patients owe the group a deductible in the first quarter, $1.23 million at $292. The group collects 60 percent at the point of service, 25 percent from statements over the following 90 days, and leaves 15 percent uncollected, $184,000, as an implicit price concession. The $9 increase moves $37,800 to patients and costs the group about $5,700. There is no 65 percent recovery for a practice paid under the physician fee schedule, because Medicare bad debt reimbursement runs through the cost report and a fee schedule practice does not file one. The real exposure is the reset itself. Patient responsibility is roughly 20 percent of Part B revenue from April to December and more than double that in January and February. The budget should phase the implicit price concession by month, not spread it evenly, or the first-quarter variance will look like a collections failure when it is a calendar.

Riverbend Post-Acute: 9,000 coinsurance days

The skilled nursing facility billed 9,000 Original Medicare coinsurance days in 2026 for days 21 through 100. At $222 the 2027 base is $2.0 million, and the $5 increase moves $45,000 to secondary insurers, the state, and patients in the same proportions the hospital uses. The facility files a cost report and can claim the 65 percent on unpaid coinsurance after the same 120-day effort, so its model is the hospital's with smaller numbers.

The group view

Consolidated, Riverbend's 2027 patient-responsibility budget is four lines per entity: secondary insurer, state Medicaid, self-pay after Medicare, and Medicare bad debt recovery. The physician fee schedule bridge and the outpatient rate bridge set the gross Medicare revenue each entity expects. This schedule sets how much of that revenue arrives from a payer other than Medicare, and the Medicare Advantage payer mix review decides how many patients sit outside the schedule altogether.

Accounting controls for the 2027 Medicare deductible reset

Source data: the 2026 Original Medicare claim detail by entity with benefit period start flags, the deductible and coinsurance amounts from the Medicare remittance advice, secondary payer identity, and dual eligible status; the patient accounting aging by financial class; the state Medicaid remittances on crossover claims; the 120-day collection log with first-bill date, each payment date, and the write-off date; the collection agency return file; three years of collection history by financial class; the CMS fact sheet and the two Federal Register notices; and the prior cost report's Exhibit 2A bad debt listing with the auditor's adjustments.

Calculation: a fixed sequence anyone can rerun. Count 2027 deductibles per entity from 2026 benefit period starts, adjusted for the volume budget. Split them by financial class. Apply each class's collection rate. The uncollected share of the patient and state classes is an implicit price concession, recorded as a reduction of net patient service revenue at the date of service and adjusted as estimates change, never as bad debt expense. The deductible is part of the transaction price; it does not change gross revenue per case, only which payer owes it. Patient receivables are point-in-time balances carried net of the concession. Medicare bad debt is a separate flow: it is claimed in the cost reporting period in which the account is written off, after the 120-day effort for non-indigent patients or the state remittance for dual eligibles, at 65 percent of the allowable amount, less sequestration. The estimated recovery is a debit to the third-party settlement receivable and a credit to Medicare revenue, trued up when the cost report is filed and settled. Write-offs go to an uncollectible receivable account that reduces revenue, which is what the 2020 rule requires and what the cost report auditor looks for, and never to the contractual allowance account.

Review: a second person reruns the claim query and lands on the same deductible counts by entity and financial class; the financial classes sum to the deductible base; no deductible is counted for a Medicare Advantage member; no Part A deductible is counted for a readmission inside an existing benefit period; the 120-day log shows a first bill within 120 days of the Medicare remittance and a restart after each payment; every crossover account has a state remittance before it appears on the bad debt listing; every account placed with an agency was returned before it was claimed; the physician group's budget carries no Medicare bad debt recovery; and the January phasing of the Part B concession is visible in the monthly budget rather than averaged away.

Decision: the CFO owns the patient-responsibility collection policy, the point-of-service collection target, and the budget method. The revenue cycle director owns the 120-day log, the must-bill process for dual eligibles, and the agency return file. The controller owns the implicit price concession estimate, the cost report settlement receivable, and the write-off account. The reimbursement manager owns Exhibit 2A and the cost report claim. Compliance owns the financial assistance policy and the indigence determinations that decide whether an account needs a collection effort at all.

Limits and common mistakes

The $40 is not the news. The January reset of the Part B deductible and the discipline of the 120-day log move far more money than the rate change, and a budget that carries only the increase will miss both.

The Part A deductible is per benefit period, not per calendar year. A readmission within 60 days of discharge carries no new deductible, so counting discharges instead of benefit period starts overstates the base, and the new amount applies to benefit periods that begin in 2027 rather than to every stay in January.

A physician practice paid under the fee schedule cannot claim Medicare bad debt. A hospital outpatient department can claim it on the facility claim. A group with both should not apply one recovery rate across entities.

Medigap coverage is not uniform. Plan G pays the Part A deductible and not the Part B deductible. Plans C and F, which paid both, closed to people who became eligible for Medicare after 2019. The secondary-payer field on the remittance, not an assumption about Medigap, decides which line an account belongs on.

Don't write Medicare bad debt off to the contractual allowance account. The 2020 rule requires an uncollectible receivable account that reduces revenue, and bad debts written off elsewhere are disallowed on audit.

The 120-day clock restarts after every payment, including a small one, and it starts from the first bill, which must go out within 120 days of the Medicare remittance. For dual eligibles, bill the state even when you know it will pay nothing; the state remittance is the evidence the auditor wants. Accounts placed with a collection agency must be closed and returned before they are claimed.

Medicare bad debt is claimed in the period the account is written off, not the period of service. A January 2027 discharge written off in June lands on the 2027 cost report and settles months after year-end, so the recovery is a settlement receivable until then and the budget should show the lag.

Riverbend is illustrative. The cost-sharing amounts are from the CMS fact sheet of November 17, 2026 and the Federal Register notices of November 19; the collection rates, documentation rates, and payer splits are the kind each entity must take from its own history, and the bad debt rules are summarized from 42 CFR 413.89 and the 2020 final rule rather than from the full Provider Reimbursement Manual.
